Liushugou Formation (C21) and associated dikes. Thirteen sites from the Liushugou Formation were collected from a continuous section in Liushugou (the Liushu Valley, \"gou\" means valley in Chinese). Six sites come from andesitic flows, tuffs, and interbedded clastics. Seven sites come from mafic dikes intruding into the bedded rocks. In many cases, the dikes were intruded into the section along existing fractures or faults. The age of the dikes is not known, although we have not seen any dike intruding into the overlying Qijiagou and Aoertu formations. The large zoned Amole pluton exposed in the northern Tucson Mountains (Figure 2) is a resurgent ring intrusion which cuts and arches the steeply dipping caldera fill upward to the east and north [Lipman, 1989]. The sequence of dacitic flows and tuffs near Safford Peak, including the dacitic neck which forms Safford Peak itself, have similar K-Ar biotite ages spanning about 28 Ma to 25 Ma [Bikerman and Damon, 1966]. The middle Tertiary volcanic rocks generally dip gently to the northeast (- 100-20 ø) and in the southeastern Tucson Mountains are basically conformable with the underlying Cretaceous rocks. This implies that most of the eastward tilting of the mountain range was associated with Tertiary faulting that may have been related to formation of the Santa Catalina core complex to the east [Lipman, 1989]. LIPMAN U.S. Geological Survey, Menlo Park, California The Tucson Mountains of southern Arizona are the site of an Upper Cretaceous caldera from which the rhyolitic Cat Mountain Tuff was erupted at about 72 Ma. Two magnetic units within the Cat Mountain Tuff are distinguished by pa!eomagnetic data in both the northern and southern Tucson Mountains. The resurgent Amole pluton (272 Ma) in the northern Tucson Mountains was emplaced soon after eruption of the Cat Mountain Tuff but cooled and was magnetized after northeastward tilting (50o-85 ø) of the adjacent caldera-fill sequence. Petrologic and pa[eomagnetic data indicate that the lower magnetic unit of the Cat Mountain Tuff caps the Silver Bell Mountains to the northwest. A previous paleoma

lockwise rotation having occurred prior to deposition of these rocks. Clockwise rotation of crustal blocks in southern Arizona likely was associated with stke-s'lip movement on major northwest trending faults in the region, and this movement may have been related to oblique subduction of oceanic plates along the western continental margin in Late Cretacdous and early Tertiary time. The available paleomagnetic data indicate that rocks in southern Arizona have not remained unrotated with respect to North America since Late Cretaceous time and that vertical axis rotations may have played an important role in the region during Laramide deformation. The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. A series of-140 to 155 Ma granites, granodiorites and diorites represent another phase of magmatic activity on Thurston Island [Storey et al., in press]. Mid- to Late Cretaceous volcanism and felsic dike intrusion occurred in the Jones Mountains [Craddock et al., 1963a], while granitic magmas were being emplaced at Lepley Nunatak [Grunow et al., 1990]. These magmatic rocks indicate that TI was along a convergent margin until the latest Cretaceous-earliest Tertiary when subduction probably ceased as a result of eastward propogation of the Pacific-Antarctic ridge [Watts et al., 1988]. The Mesozoic rocks in the Jones Mountains are unconformably overlain by glacial till and flat-lying Tertiary alkaline volcanics [Craddock et al., 1969; Rutford et al., 1972]. volcanism and felsic dike intrusion occurred in the Jones Mountains [Craddock et al., 1963a], while granitic magmas were being emplaced at Lepley Nunatak [Grunow et al., 1990]. These magmatic rocks indicate that TI was along a convergent margin until the latest Cretaceous-earliest Tertiary when subduction probably ceased as a result of eastward propogation of the Pacific-Antarctic ridge [Watts et al., 1988]. The Mesozoic rocks in the Jones Mountains are unconformably overlain by glacial till and flat-lying Tertiary alkaline volcanics [Craddock et al., 1969; Rutford et al., 1972]. The thermal event that produced the Tertiary alkalic basalts may have also created the grabenlike structure in which the Abbot Ice Shelf is found (Figure 1). The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. Triassic granodiorites (-230 Ma) at Mount Btamhall [Grunow et al., 1990] and Lower Jurassic granites (-200 Ma) in the Jones Mountains [Craddock et al., 1969; Pankhurst, 1990] indicate magmatic activity on Thurston Island in the early Mesozoic. A series of-140 to 155 Ma granites, granodiorites and diorites represent another phase of magmatic activity on Thurston Island [Storey et al., in press]. The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. Mount Bramhall Mount Btamhall consists of a medium-grained, hornblende + biotite-bearing granodiorite body with pods of finer-grained diorite schlieren. The 40Ar/39Ar analysis yielded a biotite isochron age of ~228 _+ 5 Ma, while K-At analysis on hornblende yielded ages of ~230 Ma. Two sites were drilled in the granodiorite and one in a diorite schlieren pod for a total of 18 cores. A single high-temperature component of magnetization (unblocking temperature to 670øC) was observed in these rocks and is most likely deuterically formed hematite. The granodiorite sites yielded upward pointing, north-northeast directed vectors (D= 23.3 ø, I=-63.7 ø) (Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 2/). The diorite schlieren site yielded downward pointing, south-southwest directed vectors approximately antipodal to the granodiorite (Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 2/). The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. NEW PALEOMAGNETIC DATA FROM THURSTON ISLAND 17,937 on Thurston Island crop out along two general east-west striking zones, parallel to the Abbot Ice Shelf. The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. Triassic granodiorites (-230 Ma) at Mount Btamhall [Grunow et al., 1990] and Lower Jurassic granites (-200 Ma) in the Jones Mountains [Craddock et al., 1969; Pankhurst, 1990] indicate magmatic activity on Thurston Island in the early Mesozoic. A series of-140 to 155 Ma granites, granodiorites and diorites represent another phase of magmatic activity on Thurston Island [Storey et al., in press]. Mid- to Late Cretaceous volcanism and felsic dike intrusion occurred in the Jones Mountains [Craddock et al., 1963a], while granitic magmas were being emplaced at Lepley Nunatak [Grunow et al., 1990]. These magmatic rocks indicate that TI was along a convergent margin until the latest Cretaceous-earliest Tertiary when subduction probably ceased as a result of eastward propogation of the Pacific-Antarctic ridge [Watts et al., 1988]. These magmatic rocks indicate that TI was along a convergent margin until the latest Cretaceous-earliest Tertiary when subduction probably ceased as a result of eastward propogation of the Pacific-Antarctic ridge [Watts et al., 1988]. The Mesozoic rocks in the Jones Mountains are unconformably overlain by glacial till and flat-lying Tertiary alkaline volcanics [Craddock et al., 1969; Rutford et al., 1972]. The thermal event that produced the Tertiary alkalic basalts may have also created the grabenlike structure in which the Abbot Ice Shelf is found (Figure 1). The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. If the AP, EWM, and TI blocks are joined in their present-day relative positions (rigid Weddellia), there is an overlap of the AP block with southern South America. Geosat, marine, and airborne gravity data [Sandwell and McAdoo, 1988; Bell et al., 1990] indicate that the continental margin of the Antarctic Peninsula is much narrower than necessarily inferred by the imprecise location of the shelf-slope break in ice-covered waters, and this lessens the pre-breakup overlap shown for the AP block with southern South America [Grunow et al., 1987b]. A reconstruction with the blocks separated (mosaic Weddellia) fits the geologic and paleomagnetic data better but requires a more complex opening history for the Weddell Sea basin [Grunow et al., 1987b; Lawyer and Scotese, 1987; Lawyer et al., 1991]. The majority of rock exposures from the TI block are of intrusive rocks with minor outcrops of volcanic rocks that are thought to represent evolution along a convergent margin during the Mesozoic. A more complete description of the rocks is given by Craddock et al. [1964a, 1969], Lopatin and Orlenko [1972], Wade and Wilbanks [1972], and Storey et al. [1991]. The oldest rocks known from TI are Carboniferous gneisses thought to represent the roots of a magmatic arc [Craddock et al., 1964b; Pankhurst, 1990]. KENT Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, New York The Newark basin red beds contain a secondary magnetization (the B component) acquired during the Middle Jurassic after the 50-20 ø basin-wide northwesterly dip was imparted to the strata of the basin and after most, if not all, of the limb rotation in the Jacksonwald syncline. The B component magnetization was most likely related to the same hydrothermal event which evidently remagnetized many of the igneous intrusions in the basin and reset their K/Ar systems at 175 Ma. The remagnetization of the red beds occurred over a few million years and was approximately coincident with the transition from continental rifting to seafloor spreading in the adjacent North Atlantic. The B component magnetization direction yields a paleomagnetic pole at 74øN, 96øE (K = 63, A95 = 2.6 ø, N= 50 sites) after structural correction for 1/3 of the Jacksonwald folding and none of the regional tilt. This pole supports recent evidence for a high- latitude model of Jurassic apparent polar wander for North America. We note, however, one intriguing coincidence, namely, between the results from Beja, southern Portugal [Perroud et al., 1985; Ruffet, 1990] and those from Almaden. Both have ENE declinations and upward inclinations, although those from Beja are steeper. The polarity assignment for the Beja rocks has traditionally been normal, indicating a southerly paleolatitude. Without belaboring the issue further, in view of the ambiguities, we suggest that the Almaden C component may also be of normal polarity and of Early Carboniferous age. If so, these results exist in a bit of vacuum as paleomagnetic observations for Hercynian Europe for this age are very scarce, but what seems clear is that the rotational and drift history for Iberia for this time may be much more complicated than previously thought. However, 12 sites from the southern end of the inlier, in and near the Llanelwedd quarry, yield a significantly different direction after correction for local tilt: D=176.4 ø, I=44.5 ø (k=42.4; a95=6.7ø). The Llanelwedd quarry data are anomalous with respect to both results from the northern parts of the inlier, and those obtained from approximately coeval rocks from the Shelve inlier. We have searched for an explanation for the discrepancy between the magnetization directions of the two areas and have now ruled out some possibilities, including superimposed magnetization components at one of the two areas. The Llanelwedd quarry lies within a wedge of dominantly andesitic volcanic rocks that appear only locally, and which are overlain by two unconformities that are also not present elsewhere in the inlier. One possible explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization is that the strata were not horizontal at the time of magnetization, either due to early volcano-tectonic tilting or primary dips on the flanks of a volcano. Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results fro

t horizontal at the time of magnetization, either due to early volcano-tectonic tilting or primary dips on the flanks of a volcano. Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results from Cenozoic volcanic rocks from the western United States suggest that even highly anomalous fields can be preserved virtually unchanged over a number of separate flow events. We currently regard this to be the most viable explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization. We conclude that the data from the 6 northern sites represent the best estimate of the Middle Ordovician axial dipole field for the inlier. However, 12 sites from the southern end of the inlier, in and near the Llanelwedd quarry, yield a significantly different direction after correction for local tilt: D=176.4 ø, I=44.5 ø (k=42.4; a95=6.7ø). The Llanelwedd quarry data are anomalous with respect to both results from the northern parts of the inlier, and those obtained from approximately coeval rocks from the Shelve inlier. We have searched for an explanation for the discrepancy between the magnetization directions of the two areas and have now ruled out some possibilities, including superimposed magnetization components at one of the two areas. The Llanelwedd quarry lies within a wedge of dominantly andesitic volcanic rocks that appear only locally, and which are overlain by two unconformities that are also not present elsewhere in the inlier. One possible explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization is that the strata were not horizontal at the time of magnetization, either due to early volcano-tectonic tilting or primary dips on the flanks of a volcano. Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results fro

Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results from Cenozoic volcanic rocks from the western United States suggest that even highly anomalous fields can be preserved virtually unchanged over a number of separate flow events. We currently regard this to be the most viable explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization. We conclude that the data from the 6 northern sites represent the best estimate of the Middle Ordovician axial dipole field for the inlier. However, 12 sites from the southern end of the inlier, in and near the Llanelwedd quarry, yield a significantly different direction after correction for local tilt: D=176.4 ø, I=44.5 ø (k=42.4; a95=6.7ø). The Llanelwedd quarry data are anomalous with respect to both results from the northern parts of the inlier, and those obtained from approximately coeval rocks from the Shelve inlier. We have searched for an explanation for the discrepancy between the magnetization directions of the two areas and have now ruled out some possibilities, including superimposed magnetization components at one of the two areas. The Llanelwedd quarry lies within a wedge of dominantly andesitic volcanic rocks that appear only locally, and which are overlain by two unconformities that are also not present elsewhere in the inlier. One possible explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization is that the strata were not horizontal at the time of magnetization, either due to early volcano-tectonic tilting or primary dips on the flanks of a volcano. Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results fro

Another possibility is that the Llanelwedd quarry rocks were extruded rapidly enough that the geocentric coaxial dipole field hypothesis cannot be applied. Results from Cenozoic volcanic rocks from the western United States suggest that even highly anomalous fields can be preserved virtually unchanged over a number of separate flow events. We currently regard this to be the most viable explanation for the anomalous nature of the Llanelwedd quarry magnetization. We conclude that the data from the 6 northern sites represent the best estimate of the Middle Ordovician axial dipole field for the inlier. acent to faults and breccia zones (McKnight 1935; Brockie et al. 1968). All of the faults in northern Arkansas postdate early Pennsylvanian, whereas those in Tri-State are both pre-ore and post-ore. The Mississippian limestones in the Tri-State are overlain unconformably by the Pennsylvanian Cherokee shale, which contains not only the youngest strata in the district but also small MVT deposits in limestone interbeds. These deposits in Tri-State and those in Pennsylvanian faults in northern Arkansas indicate that at least some mineralization must be Pennsylvanian or younger. Sphalerite fluid-inclusion studies indicate that freezing tem- peratures for northern Arkansas and Tri-State range from -20.8 to -23.6"' and from -23.0 to - 23.4OC respectively, corres- ponding to salinities of greater than 22 wt% salt (Roedder 1967; Leach et al. 1975). Their homogenization temperatures range from 83 to 120°C and from 83 to 132OC, respectively (Schmidt 1962; Leach et al. 1975). The similarity of the salinities, temperatures, and stratigraphic relationships led Leach et al. (1975) and Leach and Rowan (1986) to suggest that the northern Arkansas and Tri-State MVT deposits were genetically related and represented the same period of mineralization. One pilot specimen from each block was AF demagnetized in 14 steps to 160 mT and a second specimen was thermally demagnetized in 50°C or 25°C steps until the measured magnetization became erratic or fell below the noise level of the magnetometer. The specimens behaved similarly on detailed AF and thermal demagnetization. Therefore, the remaining specimens were AF demagnetized only, using at least four steps. Demagnetization paths were plotted on orthogonal vector diagrams (Zijderveld 1967) and stereograms. Paleomagnetic results Matachewan dykes The Matachewan dykes contain a well-defined remanence component that may have either of two approximately antipodal directions (Strangway 1961, 1964; Fahrig et al. 1965). One direction, designated as normal polarity (N), has a shallow positive inclination and north-northeast declination, and the opposite one is referred to as having reversed polarity (R). On the basis of partial baked-contact tests on single dykes of each polarity in the Timmins-Matachewan area (R, Pesonen 1973; N, Irving and Naldrett 1977), both components appear to be of primary origin, i.e., thermal and (or) deuteric chemical rema- nences formed during the initial cooling of the dyke. Typical responses to AF demagnetization of N and R dykes (Fig. 5) show that the component is often isolated after intensities have fallen to below 10% of the initial NRM value. In many sites, chilled margins have higher median destructive fields than coarser grained interior samples and more frequently yield well-defined characteristic component linear segments on vector diagrams. Outside the KSZ the dykes occur in lower-grade terranes and contain unclouded feldspars. Matachewan dykes within the KSZ are also fresh, contain an aluminous, blue-green amphibole, have fewer plagioclase phenocrysts, and on average are thi~er compared with their counterparts outside, which are more hydrously altered, contain a green, fibrous amphibole, and are locally abundant in felspar phenocrysts. Within the Matachewan swarm, magnetic polarity domains - areas of dominantly normal or reversed magnetization - have been identified; the boundaries of these domains correspond closely to major faults. Two of these faults form the boundaries of the KSZ and separate normal dykes within from dominantly reversed ones outside. Matachewan dykes within the KSZ are also fresh, contain an aluminous, blue-green amphibole, have fewer plagioclase phenocrysts, and on average are thi~er compared with their counterparts outside, which are more hydrously altered, contain a green, fibrous amphibole, and are locally abundant in felspar phenocrysts. Within the Matachewan swarm, magnetic polarity domains - areas of dominantly normal or reversed magnetization - have been identified; the boundaries of these domains correspond closely to major faults. Two of these faults form the boundaries of the KSZ and separate normal dykes within from dominantly reversed ones outside. The foregoing petrological and paleomagnetic observations are related to differential vertical crustal movements that have raised younger, normal-polarity Matachewan dykes (as exemplified by those within the KSZ) from a deeper crustal level and juxtaposed them against older, reversely magnetized dykes that were intruded at shallower crustal levels. fferential crustal uplift and the age and depth of emplacement of the dykes. A secondary objective is to test the extent to which the Matachew- an and Kapuskasing dykes have been involved in KSZ tecton- ics. Our study is based on paleomagnetic data from more than 600 oriented samples collected at 68 sites from the western half of the Matachewan swarm and from the Kapuskasing dykes in the vicinity of Chapleau, along Highway 101 to the west and northwards as far as Missinaibi Lake (Fig. 2). Field and analytical procedure Previous experience with Early Proterozoic dykes (Halls 1986) showed that fresh chilled margins retain a primary remanence more often than coarser grained interiors. Accord- ingly, samples were obtained from chilled margins wherever possible, with a minority taken from dyke interiors. Typically six to eight oriented samples were collected from each site with both magnetic and astro compasses. Samples were mostly field drilled along Highway 101 and block sampled elsewhere. At some sites where cross-cutting dykes were observed, as many as 20 oriented samples were obtained. The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of specimens prepared from field samples was measured on spinner magne- tometers (a modified DIGICO at the University of Toronto and a Schonstedt DSM-1 at The University of Western Ontario) and stepwise demagnetized in an alternating field (AF) having a peak intensity of 100 mT. A limited amount of thermal demagnetization was performed using a Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace. Remanence directions were obtained individually for each specimen following a procedure (Halls 1986) that uses remagnetization circles (Bailey and Halls 1984) and principal- component analysis (Kirschvink 1980; mean angular deviation values 5 10"). A summary of all structural and paleomagnetic data obtained is given in the Appendix. EarthSci. 27, 124-130 (1990) Introduction Sediments on Banks Island in the southwestern Canadian Arctic Archipelago (Fig. 1) record late Tertiary preglacial events as well as three full Quaternary continental glaciations followed or preceded by warm, nonglacial intervals. A full account of these events has been presented in Vincent (1983, 1984, 1989). Although fossil material is abundant and well preserved, obtaining chronological control on Banks Island is difficult because most sedime

of Duck Hawk Bluffs on Banks Island indicates that (i) deposits of the Worth Point Formation and those of the Banks Glaciation (Duck Hawk Bluffs Formation) are Early Pleistocene in age or older, (ii) the Brunhes-Matuyama boundary is clearly recorded within the interglacial Morgan Bluffs Formation, and (iii) a reliable paleomagnetic record can be obtained from sediments that have been subjected to permafrost conditions for extensive periods of time. Terrestrial sediments that are magnetically reversed and of Matuyarna age have also been recognized on lands bordering the Arctic Ocean - the Kap Kgbenhavn Formation in Greenland (Abrahamsen and Marcussen 1986), the older lacustrine deposits in the Old Crow Basin of the Yukon (Pearce et al. 1982), and the Gubik Formation of the Alaskan Coastal Plain (Carter and Galloway 1985) - and in the Arctic Ocean basin itself (Clarke et al. 1980; Aksu and Mudie 1985; Witte and Kent 1988). The Banks Island paleomagnetic record therefore provides a unique opportunity for correlating major Quaternary sequences found there with those of other areas. This is particularly important at this time, since many of the older sediment suites provide critical information on conditions that characterized Arctic 128 CAN. 1. EARTH SCI. VOL. 27,

Received January 25, 199 1 Revision accepted July 18, 1991 Mokowan Butte in southwestern Alberta is capped by 32 m of unconsolidated sediment comprising five tills and their associated paleosols. Previous stratigraphic work has indicated that the older tills are probably Early Pleistocene to late Tertiary in age. Paleomagnetic studies, based on 125 samples, show that the uppermost till-paleosol unit and the modem subsoil are normally magnetized, whereas the till-paleosol units from the middle of the sequence have reversed magnetization. We argue that these belong to the Brunhes and Matuyama polarity zones, respectively. The lowest part of the sequence has not been studied in detail and is generally too coarse for paleomagnetic sampling, and samples that have been obtained contain no accurate record of the paleofield. These new data, together with those from Wellsch Valley in Saskatchewan, Banks Island in the Northwest Temtories, Fort Selkirk in the Yukon, and Memtt in British Columbia, bring to five the number of early Quaternary sequences in Canada that have yielded a record of glacial sediments deposited during the Matuyama chron, and hence record glacial events prior to the last reversal of the geomagnetic field (720 ka). (Boelstorff 1978) proposed that tills 1 and 2 and their associated paleosols and till 3 were older than 2.2 Ma, that the soil on till 3 developed from about 2 to 0.9 Ma, that till 4 and its paleosol formed between 0.9 and 0.5 Ma, and finally that till 5 and its paleosol developed between 0.5 Ma and about 65 ka. Karlstrom (1987, p. 2237) reported that eight samples from a silt band between paleosols 3 and 4 at the north section were reversely magnetized, which is consistent with his age assign- ments, since this bed should fall in the Matuyama reversed polarity zone. Previous stratigraphic work has indicated that the older tills are probably Early Pleistocene to late Tertiary in age. Paleomagnetic studies, based on 125 samples, show that the uppermost till-paleosol unit and the modem subsoil are normally magnetized, whereas the till-paleosol units from the middle of the sequence have reversed magnetization. The Wathaman batholith is thought to be an ensialic magmatic arc that defines the location of the northwest-dipping THO suture zone. Thus it is an obvious target for paleomagnetic study to better understand the geometry of closure of the THO. Geology The Wathaman batholith, sometimes called the Wathaman- Chipewyan batholith, in Saskatchewan and Manitoba is a megacrystic granitoid pluton that is over 900 km long and over 150 km wide in places, making it the world's largest known Precambrian pluton (Fig. 1) (Fumerton et al. 1984). This massive monzogranite-granodiorite pluton is remarkably homogeneous and shows little evidence of multiple intrusive episodes (Lewry et al. 1981). The batholith's northwestern contact is defined by blastomylonites in the major Needle Falls ' Lithoprobe Publication 243. and Parker Lake shear zones that separate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone

parate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone is composed of intraoceanic rocks of several domains which are relicts of the Manikewan oceanic basin and extend southeastwards to the Archean Superior province (Stauffer 1984). The Wathaman batholith is comprised of richly porphyritic quartz monzonite, grading to granodiorite and granite in this study area (Lewry et al. 1980a, 1980b; Johnston 1985). The abundance and size of the microcline megacrysts decrease near the batholith's margins. A weak primary flow foliation, acquired during magmatic emplacement, is seen in the pre- ferential alignment of the megacrysts. Superimposed on the primary fabric is the main flaser and mylonite fabric associated with the shearing and compressional event that formed the Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones. The Wathaman batholith is thought to be an ensialic magmatic arc that defines the location of the northwest-dipping THO suture zone. Thus it is an obvious target for paleomagnetic study to better understand the geometry of closure of the THO. Geology The Wathaman batholith, sometimes called the Wathaman- Chipewyan batholith, in Saskatchewan and Manitoba is a megacrystic granitoid pluton that is over 900 km long and over 150 km wide in places, making it the world's largest known Precambrian pluton (Fig. 1) (Fumerton et al. 1984). This massive monzogranite-granodiorite pluton is remarkably homogeneous and shows little evidence of multiple intrusive episodes (Lewry et al. 1981). The batholith's northwestern contact is defined by blastomylonites in the major Needle Falls ' Lithoprobe Publication 243. and Parker Lake shear zones that separate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone

parate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone is composed of intraoceanic rocks of several domains which are relicts of the Manikewan oceanic basin and extend southeastwards to the Archean Superior province (Stauffer 1984). The Wathaman batholith is comprised of richly porphyritic quartz monzonite, grading to granodiorite and granite in this study area (Lewry et al. 1980a, 1980b; Johnston 1985). The abundance and size of the microcline megacrysts decrease near the batholith's margins. A weak primary flow foliation, acquired during magmatic emplacement, is seen in the pre- ferential alignment of the megacrysts. Superimposed on the primary fabric is the main flaser and mylonite fabric associated with the shearing and compressional event that formed the Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones. Dykes adjacent to the GB carry a magnetization (D = 1 lo, I = 26", a,, = 27", N = 3) that is characteristic of 2.45 Ga Matachewan dykes. Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. here for the first time, reveal that the dykes contain a dual-polarity primary remanence that varies across the swarm in both inclination and declination. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. Our data suggest that this changing trend is a secondary feature and that the western dykes, like their eastern counterparts, originally had a more uniform trend. Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. Although the signature is readily recognized as Mata- chewan, significant variations occur in both declination and inclination of the magnetization. here for the first time, reveal that the dykes contain a dual-polarity primary remanence that varies across the swarm in both inclination and declination. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. However, for dykes within and northwest of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ) a positive correlation is found between regionally averaged values of declination and dyke trend. Magnetic anisotropy Other possible causes of paleomagnetic variation are the effects of magnetic anisotropy. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke. Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. Although the signature is readily recognized as Mata- chewan, significant variations occur in both declination and inclination of the magnetization. The inclination changes are most easily explained in terms of either apparent or true wander of the geomagnetic pole, such that later dykes were intruded in a 20" steeper ambient paleofield. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. Although the signature is readily recognized as Mata- chewan, significant variations occur in both declination and inclination of the magnetization. here for the first time, reveal that the dykes contain a dual-polarity primary remanence that varies across the swarm in both inclination and declination. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. However, for dykes within and northwest of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ) a positive correlation is found between regionally averaged values of declination and dyke trend. Here the dykes appear to have suffered differential rotations about vertical axes of up to 40° since emplacement. Our data suggest that this changing trend is a secondary feature and that the western dykes, like their eastern counterparts, originally had a more uniform trend. Magnetic anisotropy Other possible causes of paleomagnetic variation are the effects of magnetic anisotropy. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke. However, typical susceptibilities are not high (0.05 SI units), and BATES AND HALLS FIG. 8. The original pattern of the Matachewan dyke swarm generated using the procedure outlined in Table 3. For essentially vertical dykes, we would expect to see a deflection in the paleomagnetic declination towards the plane of the dyke, by an amount dependent on the angle between the paleofield and dyke plane. Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. Although the signature is readily recognized as Mata- chewan, significant variations occur in both declination and inclination of the magnetization. The inclination changes are most easily explained in terms of either apparent or true wander of the geomagnetic pole, such that later dykes were intruded in a 20" steeper ambient paleofield. Hence our main purposes in resampling the site were to determine accurately the position of the Brunhes-Matuyama boundary in relation to the tephra and to investigate critically the evidence for normal horizons previously reported within the lower predominantly reversed section. These matters are of importance for dating the section and for making inferences about the distribution and migration of early Quaternary mammals across the prairies. Paleomagnetic sampling and measurement In July 1988, a section through Jaw Face was cleaned by backhoe, exposing 11 m of sediment (Fig. 2). A series of steps with vertical faces were carved with shovel and knife. Plastic cubes (2.4 cm sides; 357 altogether) were pressed into the vertical face in as continuous a fashion as possible. Measurements were made on Schonstedt spinner magnetome- ters to which were attached devices that automate specimen manipulation and data acquisition. Batches of 15 specimens can be measured unattended. The system is controlled by IBM PC's. Stepwise alternating-field (AF) demagnetization was carried out using a Schonstedt GSC-5 for fields up to 100 mT and a Sap- phire Instrument SI-4 for fields up to 180 mT. Demagnetization was carried out by treatment along three axes successively. With the exception of specimens showing very high internal disper- sion, all have been treated in at least five sequential demagneti- zation steps. Within the lower reversed section, two levels of normal polarity were described by Foster and Stalker (1976) and assigned to the Jaramillo (Doell and Dalrymple 1963) and Olduvai (Gromme and Hay 1963; Gromme 1967) subzones. Later work by Barendregt (1984) confirmed the predominantly reversed nature of the lower beds and, he argued, provided further evidence for the presence of the Jaramillo and Olduvai subzones. However, neither study was based on extensive demagnetization experiments, and few details were reported. Without a detailed assessment of demagnetization characteris- tics, these sediments cannot be used confidently as recorders of the paleofield because they have a complex history of freezing and thawing and wetting and drying which may have modified or obliterated the original magnetization. As will become clear later, accurate assessment of polarity variations can only be made after detailed sampling and analysis. Except for minor uplift, it has not been tectonically disturbed or metamorphosed, making it a good target to provide a basal Cambrian pole position. Further, there is little agreement on the Cambrian segment of the apparent polar wander path (APWP) for North America because the poles are widely scattered (Watts et al. 1980; Van der Voo 1990). Most of them come from sedimentary units, and many of these units appear to have a secondary remagnetization. Neverthe- less, a reliable Cambrian APWP would be valuable to help resolve continental reconstruction problems such as the location of the Avalon terrane relative to the craton in the Cambrian (Schenk 1978). Experimental methods Sampling Three oriented blocks were collected at each of the 29 sites, with 8 in the zinc-lead ore, 12 in the surrounding dolomite envelope, and 9 in more remote limestones of the Thumb Mountain Table Formation (Table 1). The mine is located entirely in permafrost, creating two specific sampling prob- lems. First, the walls are heavily frosted or iced, making it difficult to select and mark block samples in much of the mine. Second, blocks that may appear coherent underground may be held together by ice in fractures and so fall apart at room tem- perature. Yet another problem is that Polaris is only about 120 km from the north magnetic pole. Thus, the present Earth's magnetic field (PEMF) is virtually vertical, so a mag- netic compass is useless for block orientation. Therefore, the blocks were oriented using 1:200 scale mine plans for topo- graphic control, so their declinations are slightly less accurate than normal for most paleomagnetic studies. From three to seven specimens were drilled from each of the 87 blocks in the laboratory, yielding a total of about 450 specimens. Fluid inclusions in sphalerite indicate ore deposition temperatures in the 52- 105°C range (Jowett 1975). This corresponds to a maximum burial depth at any time of about 3 km, assuming an average geothermal gradient of about 3S°C/km. The conodont altera- tion index (CAI) about the deposit is less than 1.5, indicating that postsedimentation temperatures have not exceeded about 90°C (D. F. Sangster, unpublished data). On the other hand, the thermal demagnetization data show unblocking tempera- tures up to 550°C for the A component. This indicates that metamorphic temperatures of >400°C for about 100 Ma would have been required to reset the higher blocking temper- ature A domains (Pullaiah et al. 1975; Walton 1980). Thus the evidence rules out the possibility that a metamorphic event created a thermoviscous remanent overprint in the ores and host rocks (McCabe and Elmore 1990). By elimination the evidence shows that the host limestones were remagnetized in Late Devonian time when the ore deposit was emplaced with its dolomitic halo. This supports the concept that hot brines in the 52 - 105°C

A minor anticlinal fold on the west side of the property was used for a paleomagnetic fold test {Graham 1949) (Fig.2). The Phanerozoic sedimentary rocks of the Cornwallis Fold Belt form part of the Arctic Platform. They rest on a Pro- terozoic basement that is exposed in the Boothia Uplift, which is the southward extension of the fold belt (Fig. 1). Uplift of up to 7- 10 km in the helt is recorded in unconformities and flanking syntectonic sediments (Okulitch et a/. 1986). Origi- nally attributed to isostatic forces, uplift is now related to com- pressional deformation that produced east-dipping reverse faults and north-south-trending folds (Okultich et al. 1986; Trenin 1989). The folds are west verging with intervening east-facing monoclines. The intensity of folding diminishes eastward onto Cornwallis Island and increases westward into Parry Islands Fold Belt to give steeply overturned tight folds that are overthrust to the west. Kerr (1977) proposed four pulses of diastrophism, termed the Cornwallis Disturbance, in the (I) Early Silurian, (2) early Early Devonian, (3) late Early Devonian, and (4) Late Devonian, with pulse 1 being mild, p

The intensity of folding diminishes eastward onto Cornwallis Island and increases westward into Parry Islands Fold Belt to give steeply overturned tight folds that are overthrust to the west. Kerr (1977) proposed four pulses of diastrophism, termed the Cornwallis Disturbance, in the (I) Early Silurian, (2) early Early Devonian, (3) late Early Devonian, and (4) Late Devonian, with pulse 1 being mild, pulse 2 being strong to produce most of the uplift and folding, and pulses 3 and 4 being moderately intense to reinforce the folds initiated in pulse 2. Okulitch et al. (1986) suggested that pulses 2 and 3 were essentially one continuous pulse in the Early Devonian which produced uplift by the stacking of thrust sheets on east-dipping basement thrust faults. Miall (1986) supported the timing and suggested the Caledonian orogeny was responsible through impact suturing to the east. Thus the later Early Devonian contains a major unconfor- mity(ies), with extensive karstification likely (Okulitch et al. 1986). The host rocks occur in the Bourgeau thrust sheet of the Front Ranges (Grieve 1982). They are flat lying, and no correction of the paleomagnetic directions for geological tilt is required. The My is exposed in a very steep face and is approximately 70 m wide. Marginal contacts are subvertical and dip away from the core of the exposure (Grieve 1982). The body consists of at least eight intrusive phases, including both breccias and massive hyp- abyssal kimberlite (Hall et al. 1989). Three hypabyssal units were sampled. The Eastern Massive Phase has moderate coercivities (20-40 mT) and unblocking temperatures in the range 400 - 500°C. On orthogonal diagrams, the remanence decays linearly to the origin. Except for one hand sample, all magneti- zations are single component, and hence all have been cleaned at 500°C. The Red-Spotted and Western Massive phases have similar magnetic properties, with coercivities somewhat lower than those of the Eastern Massive Phase. Unblocking temperatures are in the range 500-550°C. Specimens from these phases yield good decay lines with alternating field (AF) demagneti- zation, and the principal magnetization, therefore. was obtained by line fitting within the range of 10-60 mT. were collected from layered Paleozoic rocks at 22 sites (26 sampleslsite) on Alfred Butte. Principal component analysis of detailed thermal demagnetization data allowed clear isolation of a characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) from 17 of these sites. Blocking temperatures to 680°C indicate that this magnetization is carried by hematite, and site -mean ChRM directions are determined with a9, < 10" for the majority of sites. On Sentine1 Mountain, samples were collected from 16 sites in layered Paleozoic volcanic and chert rocks and from a diabase sill. Thermal demag- netization revealed a ChRM in the chert and volcanic rocks with blocking temperatures to 680°C, whereas alternating-field demagnetization to 40 mT successfully isolated ChRM in the diabase sill. ChRM directions from four sites involved in a mesoscopic S-fold at Alfred Butte fail the fold test, indicating that the ChRM is a postfolding secondary remagnetization. Tests for relative age of structural tilting and remagnetization are ambiguous, with attendant uncertainties in tectonic interpre- tations. However, rock-magnetic and geologic constraints argue for a chemical remagnetization of these Paleozoic rocks in Late Triassic to Middle Jurassic time, possibly associated with structural juxtaposition of the Cache Creek and

Dans la région nord du terrane de Cache Creek, près de Atlin en Colombie-Britannique, des échantillons de roches stratifiées paléozoïques ont été prélevés pour étude paléomagnétique à 22 sites (2 6 échantillons/site) sur la butte Alfred. La principale composante qui résulte de l'examen détaillé de la désaimantation par chauffage, indique clairement pour 17 des sites étudiés une direction isolée d'aimantation rémanente caractéristique (ARca). Sixteen paleomagnetic sites (minimum 6 sampleslsite) were collected on Sentine1 Mountain within and along the margins of a 50 m wide, subvertical diabase si11 that intrudes radiolarian chert and volcanic rocks (Fig. 4). Along its upper contact, composi - tional layering in the si11 dips steeply northward and is copla- nar with bedding in the adjacent chert. Along its lower contact, the si11 follows a thin zone of chert and graded vol- canic tuff. The upper and lower contact rocks are visibly baked within 10 m of the diabase body. The baked zone is rich in hematite, some of which apparently formed as a result of si11 emplacement. Although the exact age of the diabase is unknown, field rela- tions suggest that it is only slightly younger than the submarine rocks that it intrudes. Unlike younger batholiths and dikes that crosscut stratigraphic and structural trends in the Cache Creek Group, the diabase sills strictly follow bedding in the 490 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. Numerous subsequent thermal events have affected the region. However, the remagnetization at Sentine1 Mountain and Alfred Butte probably occurred as a low-temperature chemical remagnetization rather than a high-temperature thermal remag - netization for the following reasons. Blocking temperatures of the ChRM approach the Curie temperature of hematite (680°C) and thermoviscous remag - netization would require temperatures in excess of 650°C (Pullaiah et al. 1975). Paleotemperature estimates from meta- morphic facies and conodont alteration indices (CAI) indicate that the rocks at Sentine1 Mountain and Alfred Butte have not been heated above - 550°C. Diabase and basalt from Sentine1 Mountain contain minera1 assemblages typical of prehnite- pumpellyite or low greenschist facies (albite, chlorite, clino- zoisite, pumpellyite, and sphene), corresponding roughly to temperatures in the 200-400°C range (Turner and Verhoogen 1960). Total strain at the sites, as indicated semiquantitatively by the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) of 28 samples, has been studied to test the hypothesis that deformation has rotated the remanence directions. AMS data vary considerably both between sites and within sites and show a path of progressive deformation on a Flinn diagram. There is a strong, positive correlation between the deviation of a sample’s remanence from the expected Cambrian fietd and its position along the deformation path, suggesting that finite strain/fabric development has rotated the magnetiza- tions. The study area is structurally contained in the South Mountain Anticlinorium whose southern margin forms the displacement transfer zone to the southern Appalachian Alleghenian thrust sheets (Elliott. 1976). If thrusting had continued and incorporated the Waynesboro rocks into these thrust sheets, the rotated magnetizations could have been incorrectly interpreted to result from rigid thrust sheet rotation. They have been derived primarily from the widespread ignimbritic flows and date back to the early years of paleomagnetism. A feature of paleomagnetism in the Philip- pines is the large amount of secondary magnetiza- tion encountered. In view of this we have cited more than one direction for sites, at which more than stable component was isolated. 178 In the face of the pervasive secondary magneti- zations in these rocks, an attempt has been made to use AF demagnetization characteristics to iden- tify the origin of the NRM. It is clear from standard analysis that the magnetization is carried by magnetite, the problems are to establish when it was acquired and what its significance is. The particular method utilizes plots of the ratio of NRM to saturation isothermal remanence (IRM (s)) during AF demagnetization (Fuller et al., 1988). The aim of the method is to provide an indication of the validity of the NRM from the characteristics of the magnetization, rather than simply by relying upon agreement with other re- sults prejudged to be correct. Clearly the ophiolite had been emplaced, uplifted, and was being eroded by this time. The Zambales ophio- lite is a particularly attractive paleomagnetic target because it is extensive and yet comparatively in- tact. Paleomagnetism has proved difficult in the Philippines. First, the location of successive arcs in Luzon gives rise to repeated intrusions with associated hydrothermal events, causing wide- spread secondary magnetizations. Second, the tec- tonic complexity of the region coupled with limited outcrop has led to uncertainty in tectonic correc- tions, the absence of fold tests and a general lack of structural control. Third, the low inclination at equatorial latitudes makes the demonstration of the sense of rotations more difficult than at higher latitudes. A more detailed discussion of the inter- pretation of the paieomagnetic data is therefore given than is customary. Geology of the Zambales ophiolite In a volume devoted to the Zambales ophiolite there is little need for a lengthy discussion of its geology in a paper devoted to its paleomagnetism. Hawkins (Editors), Ophiolites and Crustal Genesis in the Philippines. Tectonophysics, 168: 171-203. Paleomagnetic results are reported from 52 sites in the Zambales ophiolite. The sites provide vertical sampling from the overlying sediments, in the north and south, to layered gabbros and dunites in the Acoje and Coto mines, in the west. They extend over an area of approximately 100 by 50 km. A Late Miocene-Pliocene intrusion in the Tarlac region gives a direction marginally distinguishable from the present field indicating a small clockwise rotation. This is consistent with other indications of clockwise rotation since Late Miocene in Luzon. Early and Mid-Miocene sediments from Barlo in the north and Tarlac in the south indicate a period of rapid counter

rget because it is extensive and yet comparatively in- tact. Paleomagnetism has proved difficult in the Philippines. First, the location of successive arcs in Luzon gives rise to repeated intrusions with associated hydrothermal events, causing wide- spread secondary magnetizations. Second, the tec- tonic complexity of the region coupled with limited outcrop has led to uncertainty in tectonic correc- tions, the absence of fold tests and a general lack of structural control. Third, the low inclination at equatorial latitudes makes the demonstration of the sense of rotations more difficult than at higher latitudes. A more detailed discussion of the inter- pretation of the paieomagnetic data is therefore given than is customary. Geology of the Zambales ophiolite In a volume devoted to the Zambales ophiolite there is little need for a lengthy discussion of its geology in a paper devoted to its paleomagnetism. The reader can go elsewhere in this volume for recent views. Earlier descriptions were given by Corby (1951) and Rossman (1964). Clearly the ophiolite had been emplaced, uplifted, and was being eroded by this time. The overall eastward dip of the body is reflected by the pro- gression from tectonized peridotite in the west to the sills and flows in the east. A key step in understanding the region was taken by Taylor and Hayes (1983), who docu- mented the timing of the opening of the South China Sea. Recognition of the sea-floor anomalies demonstrated that the spreading took place be- tween 32 and 18 Ma. This demonstrates that the Zambales ophiolite cannot be from the South China Sea. The regional tectonic setting of the Zambales ophiolite has been touched upon by many authors in more general discussions of the Philippines, the Philippine Sea Plate and the South China Sea (e.g., Gervasio, 1971; Hamilton, 1979; Holloway, 1982; McCabe et al., 1982; Karig, 1983; Sarewitz and Karig, 1986; Mitchell et al., 1986). Allen (1962), using aerial photographs and limited field geologic observations, proposed that the Philippine fault zone was indeed a physiographi- tally and structurally prominent feature. Allen also stated that the pro- nounced linearity of the fault suggests that hori- zontal displacement has been the predominant motion throughout its history. In the present paper we document new paleo- magnetic and structural data from the Dunn Point Formation and describe the results of a new fold test that better constrains the age of the stable high blocking temperature magnetization in the volcanics. The previous interpretations by both groups of workers are examined in the light of these new data. Geological setting The Dunn Point Formation occurs along the Northumberland coast of mainland Nova Scotia near Arisaig (Fig. 1). The stratified rocks of the Arisaig region, including the Dunn Point Forma- tion, have been described by Boucot et al. (1974) Benson (1974), Keppie et al. (1978) and Pickerill and Hurst (1983). The Dunn Point is a bimodal sequence of volcanics some 200 m thick, consist- ing of predominantly vesicular basalt flows but including variable amounts of interlayered rhyo- lites

e overlying sedi- ments. The tops of nearly all of the flows in the Dunn Point Formation are oxidized; moreover, red soil profiles interpreted as laterites by Boucot et al. (1974) and Keppie et al. (1978), are occasionally interstratified with the volcanics. The interiors of the basalt flows also show hematite staining but in all cases the tops of flows are more extensively oxidized. This evidence suggests that the volcanics were deposited subareally and that individual flows were probably oxidized a short time after their formation. Incorporation of laterite xenoliths within less oxidized material at the base of some flows reinforces the interpretation that oxidation and formation of these red soils were very early (e.g., Keppie et al., 1978). These observations are important for the interpretation of the paleo- magnetic results for the volcanics, because they suggest that the formation of the magnetically very stable mineral hematite was essentially coeval with the formation of the volcanics. The Dunn Point strata and the overlying Arisaig Group were tilted together in post-Early Devonian time in an episode of deformation that has been correlated with the Acadian orogeny in the north- ern Appalachians (Boucot et al., 1974). (1987) obtained samples of the Dunn Point Formation from all three outcrop belts shown in Fig. 1. They likewise found a stable high blocking temperature compo- nent carried by hematite (A component of Seguin et al., 1987) in the majority of their samples, and the directions given for this component, both in situ and tilt corrected, are similar to those re- ported by Van der Voo and Johnson (1987). Yet the fold test, based on their somewhat broader distribution of sampling sites, was not significant. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained for three new sites in steeply inclined subarea1 volcanic flows of the Dunn Point Formation from the Avalon terrane of Nova Scotia. Demagnetization analysis reveals a characteristic magnetiza- tion, carried by hematite, which is similar to that reported in previous studies of this unit. Paleomagnetic results have been obtained for three new sites in steeply inclined subarea1 volcanic flows of the Dunn Point Formation from the Avalon terrane of Nova Scotia. Demagnetization analysis reveals a characteristic magnetiza- tion, carried by hematite, which is similar to that reported in previous studies of this unit. istic component of D = 344O, I = -60°, k = 68.6, ass = 4.1“ (paleopole at 2ON, 130’E) corresponds to a Late Ordovician-earliest Silurian paleolatitude for Avalon of 41°S. The latter is much higher than that predicted for the area on the basis of the cratonic North America apparent polar wander path, implying a substantial post-Ordovi- cian displacement (> 1700 km) of Avalon with respect to the craton. The Dunn Point result supports previous paleogeographic reconstructions that show Avalon together with the continental blocks of Hercynian Europe and northwestern Gondwana. Introduction The latest Ordovician-earliest Silurian Dunn Point Formation is part of the Avalon terrane in the northern Appalachians. Recently published Late Precambrian and Early Paleozoic paleo- magnetic results from this terrane (Weisse et al., 1985; Johnson and Van der Voo, 1985; 1986; Fang et al., 1986) show that it formerly occupied intermediate to high southern paleolatitudes, which contrast with the near equatorial position de- termined for North America for the same interval (e.g., Watts et al., 1980; Lynnes and Van der Voo, 1984; Dunn and Elmore, 1985). These results thus confirm the displaced nature of the Avalon ter- rane relative to North America. On the other hand, the Early Paleozoic pa

hese results thus confirm the displaced nature of the Avalon ter- rane relative to North America. Many authors have argued that such a configuration probably persisted at least through Ordovician time (e.g., Cocks and Fortey, 1982; Van der Voo, 1988). Previous paleomagnetic investigations of the Dunn Point Formation were undertaken in order to de- termine the position of Avalon relative to the major Atlantic-bordering continents in the Late Ordovician-earliest Silurian. The following evidence implies that the ob- served field directions are of primary remanent magnetizations of Late Eocene age: (1) All directions have reversed polarity. (4) The magnetic carrier is titanium-poor mag- netite, which is rarely produced in an oxygenic environment. We report new results from our paleomagnetic studies of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region in northeastern China and the Xinjiang autonomous region in northwestern &hina. Primary rna~~t~t~ons are isolated in Tertiary, Cretaceous, Late Jurassic, and Late Permian rocks, and secondary components of magnetization of Late Jurassic and Recent ages are seen in strata of Inner Mongolia. Western Junggar Basin, and part of the Tarim block, suffered widespread complete tectono-thermal remagnetization at about 280 Ma (Permian). The paleomagnetic evidence suggests that the sampled areas in Inner MongoLia have been part of the North China Block at least since Late Permian time, and the Junggar block collided with the Tarim block by Late Permian time. Our own paleomagnetic results together with available data from other parts of eastern Eurasia, suggest a tectonic model in which Kazakhstan, Europe, and Siberia collided with each other and formed the Europe-Siberia- Kazakhstan plate (EUR-SIB-KAZ) in Late Permian time. To the east, Mongolia (= Outer Mongolia), Inner Mongolia, and the North China Block were also wedged together forming the Mongolia-North China plate (MON-NC) by this time. n Asia and Western Pacific Continental Margin. Tectonophysics, 181: 43-81. We report new results from our paleomagnetic studies of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region in northeastern China and the Xinjiang autonomous region in northwestern &hina. Primary rna~~t~t~ons are isolated in Tertiary, Cretaceous, Late Jurassic, and Late Permian rocks, and secondary components of magnetization of Late Jurassic and Recent ages are seen in strata of Inner Mongolia. Western Junggar Basin, and part of the Tarim block, suffered widespread complete tectono-thermal remagnetization at about 280 Ma (Permian). The paleomagnetic evidence suggests that the sampled areas in Inner MongoLia have been part of the North China Block at least since Late Permian time, and the Junggar block collided with the Tarim block by Late Permian time. Our own paleomagnetic results together with available data from other parts of eastern Eurasia, suggest a tectonic model in which Kazakhstan, Europe, and Siberia collided with each other and formed the Europe-Siberia- Kazakhstan plate (EUR-SIB-KAZ) in Late Permian time. To the east, Mongolia (= Outer Mongolia), Inner Mongolia, and the North China Block were also wedged together forming the Mongolia-North China plate (MON-NC) by this time. These two composite contine

We reported preliminary results from these studies at several meetings (Coe et al., 1988; Zhao et al., 1988), and gave a tentative inte~retation of them in a recent article that dealt mainly with the amalgamation of the NCB and SCB (Zhao and Coe, 1989). There we proposed a simple tectonic model in which initial collision of the Chinese and Siberian blocks occurred in the Late Permian near the western end of the east-west trending South Siberian Fold Belt (Fig. 1) and progressed east- ward as the Chinese blocks rotated anticlockwise relative to Siberia during the Mesozoic. In this paper we present the detailed account of our own paleomagnetic results in the eastern (In- ner Mongolia) and western (Junggar) parts of the Central Asian Fold Belt and gather other relevant paleomagnetic data from various blocks of eastern Eurasia, some of which are not currently available in the western literature. By evaluating and com- paring the available paleomagnetic data, we refine our tectonic model for the collision and relative rotation of these blocks and illustrate semi- quantitatively the amounts of rotation involved at some key points in geologic time. 46 Fig. lc. We report new results from our paleomagnetic studies of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region in northeastern China and the Xinjiang autonomous region in northwestern &hina. Primary rna~~t~t~ons are isolated in Tertiary, Cretaceous, Late Jurassic, and Late Permian rocks, and secondary components of magnetization of Late Jurassic and Recent ages are seen in strata of Inner Mongolia. Western Junggar Basin, and part of the Tarim block, suffered widespread complete tectono-thermal remagnetization at about 280 Ma (Permian). The paleomagnetic evidence suggests that the sampled areas in Inner MongoLia have been part of the North China Block at least since Late Permian time, and the Junggar block collided with the Tarim block by Late Permian time. Our own paleomagnetic results together with available data from other parts of eastern Eurasia, suggest a tectonic model in which Kazakhstan, Europe, and Siberia collided with each other and formed the Europe-Siberia- Kazakhstan plate (EUR-SIB-KAZ) in Late Permian time. We report new results from our paleomagnetic studies of the Inner Mongolia autonomous region in northeastern China and the Xinjiang autonomous region in northwestern &hina. Primary rna~~t~t~ons are isolated in Tertiary, Cretaceous, Late Jurassic, and Late Permian rocks, and secondary components of magnetization of Late Jurassic and Recent ages are seen in strata of Inner Mongolia. Western Junggar Basin, and part of the Tarim block, suffered widespread complete tectono-thermal remagnetization at about 280 Ma (Permian). The paleomagnetic evidence suggests that the sampled areas in Inner MongoLia have been part of the North China Block at least since Late Permian time, and the Junggar block collided with the Tarim block by Late Permian time. Our own paleomagnetic results together with available data from other parts of eastern Eurasia, suggest a tectonic model in which Kazakhstan, Europe, and Siberia collided with each other and formed the Europe-Siberia- Kazakhstan plate (EUR-SIB-KAZ) in Late Permian time. To the east, Mongolia (= Outer Mongolia), Inner Mongolia, and the North China Block were also wedged together forming the Mongolia-North China plate (MON-NC) by this time. These two composite contine

(Huang, 1978; Ren et al., 1980, 1987; Wang, 1981; Li and Tang, 1983; Li et al., 1984; Zhang et al., 1984; Chen and Liang, 1985; Ji and Coney, 1985; Yang and Yang, 1985; Wang and Liu, 1986; Yang et al., 1986; Coleman, 1989; Feng et al., 1989; ~a~y~a et al., 1989). For instance, Ren et al. (1980, 1987) concluded that the various blocks within China were connected to Siberia during the Hercynian erogenic phases. Using terminology from plate tectonic theory, Li and Tang (1983), Yang and Yang (1985), and Yang et al. (1986) concluded that the sea trough between the Siberian and Chinese blocks was closed in the Late Paleozoic. Similar conclusions were also reached by analyzing paleobiogeo- graphic data (Wang, 1981; Wu, 1981; Wang and Liu, 1986). However, ever since the pioneering study by McElhi~y et al. (1981), paleomagnetic data have strongly contradicted these geological assertions for pre-Late Permian suturing of China to Siberia (see below). Moreover, there are a few geological studies as well that support a post- Permian date of amalgamation. Klimetz (1983) argued that collision between Chinese blocks and Siberia did not occur until Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous time, based mainly on his stratigraphic summary and analysis for eastern China, a Philippine Sea

We reported preliminary results from these studies at several meetings (Coe et al., 1988; Zhao et al., 1988), and gave a tentative inte~retation of them in a recent article that dealt mainly with the amalgamation of the NCB and SCB (Zhao and Coe, 1989). There we proposed a simple tectonic model in which initial collision of the Chinese and Siberian blocks occurred in the Late Permian near the western end of the east-west trending South Siberian Fold Belt (Fig. 1) and progressed east- ward as the Chinese blocks rotated anticlockwise relative to Siberia during the Mesozoic. In this paper we present the detailed account of our own paleomagnetic results in the eastern (In- ner Mongolia) and western (Junggar) parts of the Central Asian Fold Belt and gather other relevant paleomagnetic data from various blocks of eastern Eurasia, some of which are not currently available in the western literature. By evaluating and com- paring the available paleomagnetic data, we refine our tectonic model for the collision and relative rotation of these blocks and illustrate semi- quantitatively the amounts of rotation involved at some key points in geologic time. 46 Fig. lc. Introduction Most models of the early development of the Appalachian Orogen in Newfoundland require the formation and ultimate destruction of a Pre- cambrian to Early Paleozoic ocean: the Iapetus ocean (Dewey, 1969; Wilson, 1966; Stevens, 1970; Williams, 1978, 1980). The width of this ocean, prior to its closure, is a matter of some debate, but estimates based on paleomagnetic evidence (John- son and Van der Voo, 1985; Briden et al., 1988) and palinspastic restorations (Williams, 1980) yield 0040-1951/90/$03.50 0 1990 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. a minimum value between 1000 and 2000 km. Paleozoic shallow-water carbonate sequences that were deposited along the continental margin of North America facing the Iapetus Ocean (Pratt and James, 1986). These rocks suffered deforma- tion during the Taconic, Acadian, and to a lesser degree, the Alleghanian orogenies and now form an integral part of the autochthonous and parau- tochthonous stratigraphy of the northern Appa- lachians (Williams, 1978). This investigation was undertaken primarily to determine the paleolatitude of the margin prior to the closure of the Iapetus, and to document the timing of deformation and the amount of any tectonic rotations which may have occurred dur- ing the deformation. Previous paleomagnetic re- sults from Ordovician rocks of western Newfound- land include those of Beales et al. (1974) Deutsch and Rao (1977) Deutsch and Prasad (1987), and Hall and Evans (1988). The Hall and Evans (1988) study presented preliminary results from the St. George Group of Port-au-Port and these data are included in this study. Deutsch and Prasad (1987)

Tectonic setting Three main tectonic/erogenic events are ob- served in the geologic record of the northern Ap- palachians; the Taconic Orogeny (Middle-Late Ordovician), the Acadian Orogeny (Devonian), and the Alleghanian Orogeny (Carboniferous- Permian). The timing of these deformational epi- sodes is directly related to the destruction of the PALEOMAGNETIC INVESTIGATION OF LOWER ORDOVICIAN ST. The Appalachian Orogen of the Canadian Maritimes can be divided into five general tectono-stratigrapbic zones (Williams, 1978; Wil- liams, 1979, 1980; Williams and Hatcher, 1983). From west to east these are the (I) Humber Zone, (2) Dunnage Zone, (3) Gander Zone, (4) Avalon Zone, and (5) Meguma Zone. The Humber Zone of western Newfoundland contains a record of the development of a stable “Atlantic type” continen- tal margin of the Iapetus Ocean and its subse- quent deformation during the Taconic Orogeny due to the collision of the Laurentian margin with an oceanic island arc terrane (the Dunnage Zone) during the Early Paleozoic (Williams, 1980; Casey and Dewey, 1984; Casey et al., 1985). This pre- terminal collision resulted in the foundering of the previously stable continental shelf and abduction of the Humber Arm Allochthon onto the margin of the craton (Rodgers and Neale, 1963; Rodgers, 1970; Williams, 1975, 1979). Equivalents of the Cambro-Ordovi- cian carbonate sequences observed in the Humber Zone of western Newfoundland are preserved in the U.S. Appalachians, northwestern Scotland, and eastern Greenland (Williams, 1984). These are found to gener- ally correspond to the Type 1, 2, and 3 compo- nents, respectively, of this study. Results from their IRM studies of 18 specimens lead them to suggest that the B component always resides in hematite, the A component is always held in mag- netite, and that the steep component is a viscous overprint also in magnetite. The Humber Zone of western Newfoundland contains a record of the development of a stable “Atlantic type” continen- tal margin of the Iapetus Ocean and its subse- quent deformation during the Taconic Orogeny due to the collision of the Laurentian margin with an oceanic island arc terrane (the Dunnage Zone) during the Early Paleozoic (Williams, 1980; Casey and Dewey, 1984; Casey et al., 1985). The St. George Group (Schuchert and Dunbar, 1934; Knight and James, 1987) of the Humber Zone in western Newfoundland is a carbonate sequence that is entirely of Canadian age (Tremadocian-Arenigian) and forms part of the “outer limestone facies” of North American Lower Ordovician shallow-water carbonates (Knight and James, 1987). Figure 1 of Deutsch and Prasad (1987) shows that sampling in their study was concentrated at one locality near Isth- mus Bay between the NGH and NIB sites and another to the west between the NSG and NSH sites (see Fig. 1). Those authors likewise dis- covered three components of remanence, a steep downward “soft” component and two reversed components of differing orientation designated the B, and A components. These are found to gener- ally correspond to the Type 1, 2, and 3 compo- nents, respectively, of this study. Results from their IRM studies of 18 specimens lead them to suggest that the B component always resides in hematite, the A component is always held in mag- netite, and that the steep component is a viscous overprint also in magnetite. As discussed above, the present study provides evidence in support of the first point, but differs somewhat from the latter two. Rather than existing solely in mag- netite, the Type 3 component is found to be associated with both magnetite and hematite. Also, the Type 1 component, in some cases, appears to be a recent magnetization residing in goethite, while in other cases is most likely a viscous contri- bution to the NRM.
