In: W.W. Sager (Editor), Paleomagnetic Constraints on Crustal Motions. Tectonophysics, 182 (spec. sect.): 337-356. To obtain an early Ordovician paleomagnetic pole position for North America, and to determine the paleolatitude of its margin of the Iapetus Ocean prior to the Taconic orogeny, a study of the lower St. George Group (Tremadocian-Arenigian) of western Newfoundland was undertaken. Analysis of 84 oriented core samples from six localities on Port au Port Peninsula indicates that the NRM of the St. George rocks is the resultant of three distinct paleomagnetic directions. The first is a steep downward component commonly observed in the low temperature range of demagnetization (room temperature 250 o C) in virtually all samples, that roughly corresponds to the present day axial dipole field direction in situ (D = 350 O, I = 68 o ). The second is a stable component with southerly declinations and shallow-intermediate negative inclinations (D, I,, s,,u = 176 O, - 20 o ; D, &,, Eorrec,d = 173 O, - 5 O, respectively) usually seen in the range of 450-600’ C

ly corresponds to the present day axial dipole field direction in situ (D = 350 O, I = 68 o ). The second is a stable component with southerly declinations and shallow-intermediate negative inclinations (D, I,, s,,u = 176 O, - 20 o ; D, &,, Eorrec,d = 173 O, - 5 O, respectively) usually seen in the range of 450-600’ C and found in approximately 46% of the specimens. The third is a stable southeasterly, shallow-intermediate positive component (D, Ii, s,,u = 161°, 16O; D, 'tilt correcwd = 163O. 34’. respectively) generally unblocked within the 350-550 o C or 450-600 o C range which was observed in 40% of the specimens. These components of remanence are herein referred to as the Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 components, respectively. The remaining 14% of the specimens were found to be either directionally unstable to thermal demagnetization or totally overprinted by the Type 1 component. The Type 2 component is interpreted to represent a post-folding, Late Paleozoic remagnetization possibly associated with the Alleghanian Orogeny. Methods The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of samples from all sites was measured using a two- component, cryogenic magnetometer housed in a shielded room. Initial measurements were made at the paleomagnetic laboratory of the University of Texas (then in Galveston). All subsequent mea- surements were carried out at the Paleomagnetic Research Laboratory (PRL) at the University of Houston. The ambient magnetic field in the shielded room at both laboratories is approxi- mately 200-300 nT. Additional shielding around the magnetometer further reduces the field in the sensor space to less than 2 nT. Alternating field and thermal demagnetization equipment are also housed in the shielded room and further screened from the Earth’s magnetic field such that the cooling space in the oven has a residual field of about 5 nT and the AF coil space, a field of less than 1 nT. Samples from each site were demagnetized using both thermal and alternating field methods. In nearly all cases, thermal demagnetization proved to be more effective in isolating stable compo- nents of remanence although stable components were identified with alternating field demagnetiza- tion also. Samples from each site were demagnetized using both thermal and alternating field methods. In nearly all cases, thermal demagnetization proved to be more effective in isolating stable compo- nents of remanence although stable components were identified with alternating field demagnetiza- tion also. Principal component analyses (Kirsch- vink, 1980) were carried out for all temperature and AF demagnetization ranges in order to better determine the direction of each component of magnetization. section_candidates.excerpt: ethods The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of samples from all sites was measured using a two- component, cryogenic magnetometer housed in a shielded room. Initial measurements were made at the paleomagnetic laboratory of the University of Texas (then in Galveston). All subsequent mea- surements were carried out at the Paleomagnetic Research Laboratory (PRL) at the University of Houston. The ambient magnetic field in the shielded room at both laboratories is approxi- mately 200-300 nT. It falls between the 1098 Ma OS2 pole and the two poles for the Mamainse Point volcanics (MPl and MP2, Robertson, 1973; Palmer and Davis, 1987) that are directly overlain by a porphyry dated at 1086:: Ma (U/Pb zircon; Palmer and Davis, 1987). This age also agrees with the U/PI, zircon results of Heaman and Machado (1987) who found that the episode III rocks of Mitchell and Platt (1982) were emplaced at about 1098 Ma which include most of these sites. Thus the C component appears to be primary and to record the cooling of magmatic episode III in the Coldwell complex. Several problems now appear for both petro- logic models. One C component site (28) is in x2 ferroaugite syenite that both Mitchell and Platt (1982) and Currie (1980) assigned to episode I. The site could well have been remagnetized when the episode II or III rocks, depending on model, were intruded next to this site. The Coldwell Complex is a large multiphase alkaline intrusion on the north shore of Lake Superior. It was emplaced into Archean metavolcanics of the Superior Province in at least three distinct magmatic episodes during the Late Precambrian, giving isotopic ages ranging from 1010 to 1188 Ma. Detailed AF and thermal dema~e~tion was done on 416 specimens from 33 sites representing all petrologic phases. Additional data are included from an unpub~sh~ 1972 study by W.A. Robertson. The oldest magnetic component, PCA, was found in 19 episode I sites with a reversed mean direction of D = 121.00, Z = - 70.9O (K = 104, ass = 3.3’). The uplift magnetisation record in the central Scandinavian Caledonides: results from basic igneous complexes. Tectonophysics, 184: 137-156. To identify the palaeomagnetic record acquired during slow post-erogenic uplift and cooling in the central part of the Scandinavian Caledonides we have investigated four separated synorogenic basic complexes in the Middle and Upper Allochthons. A shallow N-S axis of magnetisation is common to three of these bodies and therefore postdates all major tectonism. It is defined in the Mesjoen Gabbro (D/I = 7’/3O, N = 23 samples, ass = S.O”), in the Sulitjelma Gabbro (D/I=20°/-9O, N=22samples, av5= 6.6O) and the R&na norite (D/I = 9O/- 16O, N = 19 samples, ag5 = 7.9”). No vestige of this uplift remanence is recognised in the Lyngen Gphiolite, where a characteristic remanence of D/Z = 65 O/43O (N = 19 samples, a,, = 10.6 o ) is recorded. The possibility that the N-S shallow axis of magnetisation is of mid-Carboniferous age, is considered and rejected. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. It cor

This possibility was suggested by some resuIts of the studies by Abrahamsen et al. (1979) and Bylund and Zeilman (1980) and has been further discussed by Abrahamsen (1985). Since local field control cannot generally isolate tectoni- cally-influenced magnetisation within individual bodies, in this study we have investigated four separated basic units to isolate that common part of the remanence record in the orogen acquired during the post-erogenic cooling. Geological setting The Scandinavian Caledonides comprise a metamorphosed nappe pile stacked by thrust movements directed NW-SE onto the Fenno- scandian (Baltic) Precambrian platform (Fig. 1) in an erogenic event culminating in Middle- Upper Silurian times (Roberts and Gee, 198s). The Uppermost Allochthon com- prises nappes incorporating both metamorphic basement and a range of supracrustal rocks. A variety of synorogenic granites and the Masjoen Gabbro of this study have been emplaced into these nappes. Nappe emplacement was succeeded by uplift, erosion and deposition in Early and Middle Devonian times of molasse deposits in fault controlled basins; there were, in turn, in- fluenced by an episode of folding, thrusting and low grade metamorphism (the Solundian episode) in late Devonian to Early Carboniferous times. The uplift magnetisation record in the central Scandinavian Caledonides: results from basic igneous complexes. Tectonophysics, 184: 137-156. To identify the palaeomagnetic record acquired during slow post-erogenic uplift and cooling in the central part of the Scandinavian Caledonides we have investigated four separated synorogenic basic complexes in the Middle and Upper Allochthons. A shallow N-S axis of magnetisation is common to three of these bodies and therefore postdates all major tectonism. It is defined in the Mesjoen Gabbro (D/I = 7’/3O, N = 23 samples, ass = S.O”), in the Sulitjelma Gabbro (D/I=20°/-9O, N=22samples, av5= 6.6O) and the R&na norite (D/I = 9O/- 16O, N = 19 samples, ag5 = 7.9”). No vestige of this uplift remanence is recognised in the Lyngen Gphiolite, where a characteristic remanence of D/Z = 65 O/43O (N = 19 samples, a,, = 10.6 o ) is recorded. The possibility that the N-S shallow axis of magnetisation is of mid-Carboniferous age, is considered and rejected. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. It cor

me remanence components have survived the meta- morphism of the nappe pile and record tectonic displacements during emplacement of the nappes in the culminating (Scandian: Silurian-Early De- vonian, ca. 420-400 Ma) phases of erogenic defor- mation. This possibility was suggested by some resuIts of the studies by Abrahamsen et al. (1979) and Bylund and Zeilman (1980) and has been further discussed by Abrahamsen (1985). Since local field control cannot generally isolate tectoni- cally-influenced magnetisation within individual bodies, in this study we have investigated four separated basic units to isolate that common part of the remanence record in the orogen acquired during the post-erogenic cooling. Geological setting The Scandinavian Caledonides comprise a metamorphosed nappe pile stacked by thrust movements directed NW-SE onto the Fenno- scandian (Baltic) Precambrian platform (Fig. 1) in an erogenic event culminating in Middle- Upper Silurian times (Roberts and Gee, 198s). The nappes are grouped into four major complexes which comprise the outcrop from east to west of the Lower, Middle, Upper and Uppermost Alloch- Lyngen Gabbro -...__ K?; ~~SulitjtAma Ophiolite 3%X31 he& Fongen Hyllirtgen Gabbro Fig. 1. n) tectonic episodes and the metamorphic grade reaches upper amphibolite facies or higher. The Uppermost Allochthon com- prises nappes incorporating both metamorphic basement and a range of supracrustal rocks. A variety of synorogenic granites and the Masjoen Gabbro of this study have been emplaced into these nappes. Nappe emplacement was succeeded by uplift, erosion and deposition in Early and Middle Devonian times of molasse deposits in fault controlled basins; there were, in turn, in- fluenced by an episode of folding, thrusting and low grade metamorphism (the Solundian episode) in late Devonian to Early Carboniferous times. The possibility that the N-S shallow axis of magnetisation is of mid-Carboniferous age, is considered and rejected. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. It corresponds closely to an axis of magnetisation extensively represented within the metamorphic Caledonides and Scotland and believed to record a post-tectonic thermochemical event. Subordinate components record Mesozoic overprinting events and relict Caledonian magnetisations which have escaped replacement during this thermo-tectonic event. The latter collectively imply a rapid movement from high to low palaeolatitudes in Late Ordovician and Early Silurian times. The uplift magnetisation record in the central Scandinavian Caledonides: results from basic igneous complexes. Tectonophysics, 184: 137-156. To identify the palaeomagnetic record acquired during slow post-erogenic uplift and cooling in the central part of the Scandinavian Caledonides we have investigated four separated synorogenic basic complexes in the Middle and Upper Allochthons. A shallow N-S axis of magnetisation is common to three of these bodies and therefore postdates all major tectonism. It is defined in the Mesjoen Gabbro (D/I = 7’/3O, N = 23 samples, ass = S.O”), in the Sulitjelma Gabbro (D/I=20°/-9O, N=22samples, av5= 6.6O) and the R&na norite (D/I = 9O/- 16O, N = 19 samples, ag5 = 7.9”). No vestige of this uplift remanence is recognised in the Lyngen Gphiolite, where a characteristic remanence of D/Z = 65 O/43O (N = 19 samples, a,, = 10.6 o ) is recorded. The possibility that the N-S shallow axis of magnetisation is of mid-Carboniferous age, is considered and rejected. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. It cor

This possibility was suggested by some resuIts of the studies by Abrahamsen et al. (1979) and Bylund and Zeilman (1980) and has been further discussed by Abrahamsen (1985). Since local field control cannot generally isolate tectoni- cally-influenced magnetisation within individual bodies, in this study we have investigated four separated basic units to isolate that common part of the remanence record in the orogen acquired during the post-erogenic cooling. The Uppermost Allochthon com- prises nappes incorporating both metamorphic basement and a range of supracrustal rocks. A variety of synorogenic granites and the Masjoen Gabbro of this study have been emplaced into these nappes. Nappe emplacement was succeeded by uplift, erosion and deposition in Early and Middle Devonian times of molasse deposits in fault controlled basins; there were, in turn, in- fluenced by an episode of folding, thrusting and low grade metamorphism (the Solundian episode) in late Devonian to Early Carboniferous times. The uplift magnetisation record in the central Scandinavian Caledonides: results from basic igneous complexes. Tectonophysics, 184: 137-156. To identify the palaeomagnetic record acquired during slow post-erogenic uplift and cooling in the central part of the Scandinavian Caledonides we have investigated four separated synorogenic basic complexes in the Middle and Upper Allochthons. A shallow N-S axis of magnetisation is common to three of these bodies and therefore postdates all major tectonism. It is defined in the Mesjoen Gabbro (D/I = 7’/3O, N = 23 samples, ass = S.O”), in the Sulitjelma Gabbro (D/I=20°/-9O, N=22samples, av5= 6.6O) and the R&na norite (D/I = 9O/- 16O, N = 19 samples, ag5 = 7.9”). No vestige of this uplift remanence is recognised in the Lyngen Gphiolite, where a characteristic remanence of D/Z = 65 O/43O (N = 19 samples, a,, = 10.6 o ) is recorded. The possibility that the N-S shallow axis of magnetisation is of mid-Carboniferous age, is considered and rejected. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. To identify the palaeomagnetic record acquired during slow post-erogenic uplift and cooling in the central part of the Scandinavian Caledonides we have investigated four separated synorogenic basic complexes in the Middle and Upper Allochthons. A shallow N-S axis of magnetisation is common to three of these bodies and therefore postdates all major tectonism. It is defined in the Mesjoen Gabbro (D/I = 7’/3O, N = 23 samples, ass = S.O”), in the Sulitjelma Gabbro (D/I=20°/-9O, N=22samples, av5= 6.6O) and the R&na norite (D/I = 9O/- 16O, N = 19 samples, ag5 = 7.9”). No vestige of this uplift remanence is recognised in the Lyngen Gphiolite, where a characteristic remanence of D/Z = 65 O/43O (N = 19 samples, a,, = 10.6 o ) is recorded. Instead it is attributed to the interval of post-tectonic cooling of the Caledonian nappe pile between synorogenic events dated ca.. 420 Ma and the uplift to surface levels defined by later Devonian events. Introduction The Jura mountains (Folded Jura) in northern Switzerland and eastern France formed as a classi- cal foreland belt in the Late Miocene during the last Alpine compression. The arcuate shape of the mountain belt is bound towards the north and west by the Oligocene Rhine-Bresse graben sys- tem. Oligocene normal faulting affected the sedi- ments as well as the basement of the younger Folded Jura. Folds and thrusts are restricted to the Mesozoic cover which is separated by Triassic evaporites from the Paleozoic basement. Folds and thrusts are restricted to the Mesozoic cover which is separated by Triassic evaporites from the Paleozoic basement. The over- thrusts and folds strike E-W in the eastern part and bend in an almost continuous manner to a N-S trend in the western regions (Fig. 1). The Tabular Jura is the aut~hthonous foreland to the north and has been mainly affected by Oligocene normal faulting. Thick- and thin-skinned tectonic models have been developed in order to explain the formation of the arcuate shape of the Jura mountains (see Laubscher, 1980). The tuck-sunned models pos- tulate sinistral strike-slip faults in the basement and en-echelon folds in the sediments above (Pavoni, 1961, We~mann, 1963). A consequence of these thick-skinned models is anticlockwise rota- tion of the sedimentary cover in the Folded Jura. Pavoni’s (1961) model requires an anticlockwise rotation of about 15 degrees, whereas 20 degrees of rotation are necessary to satisfy Wegmann’s (1963) reconstruction. magnetic studies have underscored the importance of recognizing remagnetizations (Van der Voo, 1989). Many of the observations of Late Paleozoic remagnetizations are in sedimentary rocks of the central and southern Appalachians where defor- mation associated with the Alleghenian orogeny was most penetrative (Hatcher, 1987) but docu- mented cases extend to relatively undeformed (Craddock and van der Pluijm, 1989) sedimentary rocks of the interior of the continent (Suk et al., 1989). While the method by which rocks are re- magnetized is not completely understood, diagene- sis or fluid-induced growth of significant mag- netite or hematite appears to be the most often cited method for remagnetizing sedimentary rocks (McCabe et al., 1983, 1984; Miller and Kent, 1988; McCabe and Elmore, 1990). Remagnetization of volcanic rocks is even less well understood. The Jim Pond Formation ex- hibits mineral assemblages typical of lowest greenschist facies metamorphism (Boudette, 1982). Heizler and Lux (1988), who dated plutons in the area and modeled the cooling history of the Chain of Ponds Pluton (see also De Yoreo et al., 1989), estimated the ambient temperature to be 350°C in the late Middle Devonian. The Jim Pond Formation ex- hibits mineral assemblages typical of lowest greenschist facies metamorphism (Boudette, 1982). Heizler and Lux (1988), who dated plutons in the area and modeled the cooling history of the Chain of Ponds Pluton (see also De Yoreo et al., 1989), estimated the ambient temperature to be 350°C in the late Middle Devonian. With the average cool- ing rate of 2” to 3”C/Ma obtained by Heizler and Lux (1988), the temperature by the late Carboniferous would be insufficient (ca. 200°C) to cause thermal resetting of magnetites with labora- tory blocking temperatures of 500-600°C (Pul- laiah et al., 1975; Middleton and Schmidt, 1982). The nearest evidence of a Carboniferous heat source is southeast of the study area near the Sebago Batholith (U-Pb age, 325 + 3 Ma; Aleinikoff et al., 1985) where Lux and Guidotti (1985) reported evidence for Late Paleozoic meta- morphism. The age for the metamorphism coin- cides with the age estimate for the paleomagnetic pole (Late Carboniferous) and, thus, the remagne- tization event. Component II is a result of a widespread late Paleozoic remagnetization event which temporally coincides with the Alleghenian orogeny. Acadian erogenic activity is most extensive in the northern Appalachians, (Williams, 1984) and the intrusion of plutonic rocks dated as Middle Devonian (e.g., Big Island Pond Pluton, Spider Lake Granite and the Chain of Ponds Pluton; Heizler and Lux, 1988; De Yoreo et al., 1989) provides a favorable environment for the acquisi- tion of a partial thermo-remanent magnetization (pTRM). However, Component III is carried by hematite, whose high unblocking temperatures in- dicate that the Acadian remagnetization must be a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM). The different carriers of the magnetization for compo- nents II and III (magnetite and hematite, respec- tively) and the estimates of post-Acadian tempera- tures discussed above explain the survival of Com- ponent III through the Late Paleozoic remagneti- zation event. Implications for other Appalachian paleomagnetic studies Comparison of the in-situ mean of Component III (Acadian remagnetization) with previous paleomagnetic results from volcanic rocks in the northern Appalachians has provided some new insights. Samples were collected from ten sites of the Late Cambrian-Early Ordovician Jim Pond Formation for paleomagnetic study. Stepwise thermal demagnetization reveals three separable components of magnetization. . Though not statistically significant, for Components II and III the precision parameter, k, decreases and the as5 increases when tilt-correction is applied, suggesting that both are post-folding magnetizations. Component II, without tilt correction, has a corresponding paleomagnetic pole located at 43ON, 130” E (dp, dm = 4.3”, 8.6 o ). which falls near the Late Carboniferous segment of the Laurentian Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP). Component III, without tilt correction, has a corresponding pole located at 32”N. 98”E (dp, dm = 4.7O, 7.8”) which falls near the Lower-Middle Devonian segment of the APWP. We conclude that the Jim Pond Formation has undergone two Paleozoic remagnetization events, one in the Early to Middle Devonian and a second one in the Late Paleozoic. The ages of these remagnetizations coincide with the timing of major erogenic activity in the area, i.e. the Acadian and Alleghenian, respectively. The remagnetization event associated with the Acadian pulse can be recognized in other paleomagnetic investigations in the northern Appalachians. Many of the observations of Late Paleozoic remagnetizations are in sedimentary rocks of the central and southern Appalachians where defor- mation associated with the Alleghenian orogeny was most penetrative (Hatcher, 1987) but docu- mented cases extend to relatively undeformed (Craddock and van der Pluijm, 1989) sedimentary rocks of the interior of the continent (Suk et al., 1989). While the method by which rocks are re- magnetized is not completely understood, diagene- sis or fluid-induced growth of significant mag- netite or hematite appears to be the most often cited method for remagnetizing sedimentary rocks (McCabe et al., 1983, 1984; Miller and Kent, 1988; McCabe and Elmore, 1990). Remagnetization of volcanic rocks is even less well understood. The Jim Pond Formation ex- hibits mineral assemblages typical of lowest greenschist facies metamorphism (Boudette, 1982). Heizler and Lux (1988), who dated plutons in the area and modeled the cooling history of the Chain of Ponds Pluton (see also De Yoreo et al., 1989), estimated the ambient temperature to be 350°C in the late Middle Devonian. nt, 1988; McCabe and Elmore, 1990). Remagnetization of volcanic rocks is even less well understood. The Jim Pond Formation ex- hibits mineral assemblages typical of lowest greenschist facies metamorphism (Boudette, 1982). Heizler and Lux (1988), who dated plutons in the area and modeled the cooling history of the Chain of Ponds Pluton (see also De Yoreo et al., 1989), estimated the ambient temperature to be 350°C in the late Middle Devonian. With the average cool- ing rate of 2” to 3”C/Ma obtained by Heizler and Lux (1988), the temperature by the late Carboniferous would be insufficient (ca. 200°C) to cause thermal resetting of magnetites with labora- tory blocking temperatures of 500-600°C (Pul- laiah et al., 1975; Middleton and Schmidt, 1982). The nearest evidence of a Carboniferous heat source is southeast of the study area near the Sebago Batholith (U-Pb age, 325 + 3 Ma; Aleinikoff et al., 1985) where Lux and Guidotti (1985) reported evidence for Late Paleozoic meta- morphism. The age for the metamorphism coin- cides with the age estimate for the paleomagnetic pole (Late Carboniferous) and, thus, the remagne- tization event. Acadian erogenic activity is most extensive in the northern Appalachians, (Williams, 1984) and the intrusion of plutonic rocks dated as Middle Devonian (e.g., Big Island Pond Pluton, Spider Lake Granite and the Chain of Ponds Pluton; Heizler and Lux, 1988; De Yoreo et al., 1989) provides a favorable environment for the acquisi- tion of a partial thermo-remanent magnetization (pTRM). However, Component III is carried by hematite, whose high unblocking temperatures in- dicate that the Acadian remagnetization must be a chemical remanent magnetization (CRM). The different carriers of the magnetization for compo- nents II and III (magnetite and hematite, respec- tively) and the estimates of post-Acadian tempera- tures discussed above explain the survival of Com- ponent III through the Late Paleozoic remagneti- zation event. One hundred sixty-five oriented hand samples were collected from 55 sites in the Mintum Formation located between Wellsville and Howard, Colorado, in an attempt to locate the base of the Permo-Carboniferous Reversed Superchron (PCRS) in western North America. After the samples were demagnetized using thermal and alternating field cleaning techniques, the normal polarity magnetizations (which marks the base of the Permo-Carboniferous Reversed Superchron (PCRS)) were not found in the Mintum Formation. Description and geological setting of area investi- gated Outcrops of the Mintum Formation were sam- pled in the Arkansas River Valley and its trib- utaries between Wellsville, and Howard, Fremont County, Colorado (Fig. 1).
